metadata.title: Custom Software Lifecycle Residuality Stress Test
metadata.description: Six hypothetical outside changes test the proposed model. All residues are candidates; none is claimed to have been implemented or survived by Dawn. No probability or likelihood is assigned.
metadata.naiveArchitecture: Independent projects produce client software, then hand it to support. Platform versions, quality records, reusable know-how and client obligations remain scattered across specialists and tools. It assumes stable dependencies, smooth handover and available key people.
metadata.residualArchitecture: Client-scoped version, ownership, evidence and recovery records connect discovery, build, operation and transfer. Reusable patterns carry provenance, dependency changes trigger targeted evaluation, and human client authority remains explicit.

stressors.name: A shared dependency is compromised across multiple client services
stressors.detection: An upstream advisory or observed artifact anomaly maps to deployed versions in several separately contracted client environments.
stressors.attractor: Clients need different response windows and maintenance approvals, while shared expertise is overloaded by simultaneous incidents.
stressors.businessReaction: Identify exposed versions and clients, assign separate incident owners, prioritize by actual user impact, test bounded replacements and communicate under each agreement.
stressors.residue: A maintained exposure-to-client map, prioritized response playbooks and independently rehearsed patch/rollback cohorts become part of normal release and service records.

impacts.effect: Include multi-client correlated incidents in recovery planning.
Use deployed-version evidence to bound incident scope.
Compare patch and rollback against client-specific constraints.
Measure recovery separately by service severity and agreement.
Make exposure visibility and response coverage explicit in lifecycle agreements.
Reserve an expedited but reviewed maintenance path.
Link upstream exposure to actual client versions.
Coordinate workload and client updates across separate incidents.
Incident readiness becomes a specific sourcing comparison criterion.

stressors.name: A device platform change prevents a critical user journey
stressors.detection: A platform beta, distribution rejection or crash pattern shows that a supported user cohort will lose a priority task.
stressors.attractor: The client’s launch or ongoing access depends on a platform timeline outside the delivery team’s control.
stressors.businessReaction: Test representative versions early, reserve review time, prepare a compatible release and communicate a workable assisted or alternate channel where available.
stressors.residue: A versioned device-support matrix, distribution-readiness evidence and task-specific fallback plan persist across future releases.

impacts.effect: Preserve task access when the usual device path fails.
Design interruption recovery and alternatives around the actual task.
Retain safe state and communicate available next steps.
Track interruption recovery on affected cohorts.
Include platform distribution dependencies in accepted scope.
Treat compatibility evidence and distribution timing as launch prerequisites.
Maintain supported versions and recovery behavior.
Own compatibility remediation with the client product owner.

stressors.name: A client or assessor requires evidence that the release record cannot currently provide
stressors.detection: A client review identifies missing requirement traceability, unsupported intended-use assumptions or an unassessed change.
stressors.attractor: Release or renewal cannot proceed until the responsible client authority has a defensible evidence chain.
stressors.businessReaction: Clarify the actual obligation with competent client roles, locate affected requirements and risks, close evidence gaps and obtain the required human decision.
stressors.residue: A maintained impact graph and versioned evidence-export profile prevent assurance from becoming a last-minute reconstruction exercise.

impacts.effect: Preserve evidence through normal changes and supplier transitions.
Assess the effect of source, model and code changes.
Track approved impact-assessment coverage.
Define evidence deliverables and client decision rights at engagement start.
Reject incomplete packs before the external review.
Maintain traceable controls and approval records.
Facilitate closure while the client retains release authority.
Compare domain expertise and reviewable deliverables in the relevant healthcare scope.

stressors.name: An AI model or knowledge source becomes unavailable or unacceptable
stressors.detection: A provider change, access-policy decision, evaluation regression or withdrawal of a source owner’s permission invalidates the approved source/model combination.
stressors.attractor: The client must preserve useful assistance without silently changing its evidence, access or intended-use boundaries.
stressors.businessReaction: Freeze promotion, fall back to approved search or human support, validate a replacement source/model combination and obtain client review before widening use.
stressors.residue: Provider-independent evaluation sets, explicit source rights, versioned combinations and a tested fallback persist as owned client-service assets.

impacts.effect: Keep trusted behavior and knowledge ownership through provider changes.
Re-evaluate each replacement against retained expectations.
Use unsupported-answer rate as a release guardrail.
Specify source/model substitution and fallback responsibilities.
Require evidence, authorization and human escalation for the changed combination.
Make a replacement comparable to the last approved version.
Support an approved fallback without mixing client knowledge.
Coordinate content-owner and client-quality approval.

stressors.name: Specialist turnover during a group integration threatens existing commitments
stressors.detection: Capacity reviews reveal a critical skill with no deputy, delayed knowledge transfer or conflicting delivery and support commitments.
stressors.attractor: Group integration and growth increase demand while existing clients still expect uninterrupted accountability and confidentiality.
stressors.businessReaction: Map client obligations before restructuring, assign accountable backups, protect maintenance capacity and verify knowledge transfer through working examples.
stressors.residue: A maintained skill-to-obligation map, receiver-verified transfer records and provenance-reviewed shared assets persist after the organizational change.

impacts.effect: Scale only with sustainable capacity and client continuity.
Verify maintainability and rights before sharing or transferring assets.
Require named backup coverage for critical obligations.
Base commitments on verified expertise and available capacity.
Review existing obligations before assigning new work.
Surface unstaffed commitments and maintenance load.
Publish only maintainable, legally reusable assets.
Own commitment visibility without overriding client acceptance.

stressors.name: A client mandates a change of hosting or delivery partner
stressors.detection: A renewal, procurement decision, cost review or supplier policy requires a receiver to take over within a fixed transition window.
stressors.attractor: The client needs working service continuity and access to its assets, while license and data-processing constraints limit what can transfer.
stressors.businessReaction: Confirm rights and responsibilities, assemble the transfer pack, rehearse receiver-run build and restoration, overlap support and close outgoing access after acceptance.
stressors.residue: Transferable build and restore evidence, explicit IP/license inventory and verified receiver readiness become maintained delivery artifacts.

impacts.effect: Make client control observable during a real sourcing change.
Accept transfer based on demonstrated receiver capability.
Require a receiver-run build and restore for completed transfers.
Include realistic exit choices in lifecycle investment advice.
Separate verified readiness from document delivery alone.
Track recipient evidence, rights and residual exceptions.
Coordinate support overlap and access transition.
Internal operation becomes a viable alternative only after readiness is demonstrated.
